claims.text: In-situ substrate preheating during additive manufacturing minimizes thermal gradients.
Minimizing thermal gradients lowers residual stresses in additively manufactured AlCrFeNiSi components.
Minimizing thermal gradients improves the mechanical properties of additively manufactured AlCrFeNiSi components.
The proposed intervention is to maintain the build substrate at approximately 550°C during processing.
The proposed processing scope is miniature components with feature sizes up to approximately 10 mm, produced under an inert atmosphere by laser powder bed fusion or a similar method.
A reduced temperature gradient during layer solidification produces a more homogeneous microstructure.
A reduced temperature gradient during layer solidification produces fewer phase boundaries.
A reduced temperature gradient during layer solidification reduces accumulated residual stress.
Maintaining an elevated substrate temperature reduces the cooling rate.
Maintaining an elevated substrate temperature minimizes differential thermal contraction.
Differential thermal contraction during additive manufacturing generates residual stresses.
The controlled thermal environment promotes more uniform solidification.
More uniform solidification preserves mechanical integrity.
Substrate preheating reduces processing complexity by reducing the need for stress-relief post-treatments.
Preheated builds will have statistically significantly lower residual stresses than conventionally processed builds.
Preheated builds will have more uniform microstructural features than conventionally processed builds.
Preheated builds will exhibit improved tensile strength and ductility relative to conventionally processed builds.
Conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing produces components with elevated residual stresses and degraded mechanical properties that require additional post-processing.
The benefits are expected to apply to miniature components because uniform temperature control is feasible at that scale.
The intervention may be less effective for larger or complex geometries because maintaining a uniform preheat temperature is more difficult.
